subproblem.title: Mean deviation is bounded by the double-integral oscillation on a set of volume 1
subproblem.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, let S ⊆ Euclid (m + 1) be any set with Lebesgue measure vol(S) = 1, and let u : Euclid (m + 1) → ℝ be integrable on S. Then, with c := ∫_S u, ∫_{x∈S}|u(x) − c| dx ≤ ∫_{x∈S}∫_{y∈S}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (S : Set (Euclid (m + 1))) (u : Euclid (m + 1) → ℝ), volume S = 1 → IntegrableOn u S → ∫ x in S, |u x - ∫ y in S, u y| ≤ ∫ x in S, ∫ y in S, |u x - u y|
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof (c := ∫_{Q₁} u, "u(x) − c = ∫_{Q₁}(u(x) − u(y)) dy, hence |u(x) − c| ≤ ∫_{Q₁}|u(x) − u(y)| dy; integrate"), stated for an arbitrary set S of volume 1. The integrability of the inner integral is step 1 of the parent proof.

Notation. Euclid (m + 1) with Lebesgue measure vol. μ := vol restricted to S (Measure.restrict, defined for every set S; for measurable A, μ(A) = vol(A ∩ S)). Apart from μ being a measure, the only property of μ used below is μ(univ) = vol(S) (Measure.restrict_apply_univ). Integrals ∫ … dμ are exactly the set integrals ∫_S … in the statement. c := ∫ u dμ = ∫_S u.

1. μ is a probability measure. μ(univ) = vol(S) = 1 (Measure.restrict_apply_univ, valid for every set S). In particular μ is finite, so constants are μ-integrable, with ∫ b dμ = μ(univ)·b = b. By hypothesis u ∈ L¹(μ).
2. Integrability on the product. On μ ⊗ μ the functions (x, y) ↦ u(x) and (x, y) ↦ u(y) are integrable (Integrable.comp_fst / Integrable.comp_snd, using that μ is finite: they are a.e.-strongly measurable as compositions of u with the coordinate projections, and by Tonelli ∫∫|u(x)| dμ(y) dμ(x) = μ(univ)·∫|u| dμ < ∞, symmetrically for u(y)). Hence F(x, y) := |u(x) − u(y)| is μ⊗μ-integrable (difference, then absolute value). By Fubini (Integrable.integral_prod_left), h(x) := ∫ |u(x) − u(y)| dμ(y) is a μ-integrable function of x.
3. Pointwise bound. Fix x. The function y ↦ u(x) − u(y) is μ-integrable (a constant minus u), and by linearity and step 1, ∫ (u(x) − u(y)) dμ(y) = μ(univ)·u(x) − ∫ u dμ = u(x) − c. Hence |u(x) − c| = |∫ (u(x) − u(y)) dμ(y)| ≤ ∫ |u(x) − u(y)| dμ(y) = h(x) (the absolute value of an integral is at most the integral of the absolute value; abs_integral_le_integral_abs).
4. Integration. The function x ↦ |u(x) − c| is nonnegative and pointwise ≤ h(x), and h is μ-integrable by step 2. By monotonicity of the integral (integral_mono_of_nonneg: nonnegative left side, integrable right side, pointwise inequality), ∫ |u(x) − c| dμ(x) ≤ ∫ h dμ = ∫_{x∈S}∫_{y∈S}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx. With c = ∫_S u this is the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: μ := vol|S satisfies μ(univ) = vol(S) = 1, so μ is a probability measure and u ∈ L¹(μ).
Fubini: |u(x) − u(y)| is μ⊗μ-integrable, so h(x) := ∫_S|u(x) − u(y)| dy is integrable on S.
Since μ(univ) = 1, u(x) − c = ∫_S (u(x) − u(y)) dy, so |u(x) − c| ≤ h(x).
Integrating the nonnegative function |u − c| ≤ h over S gives ∫_S|u − c| ≤ ∫_S∫_S|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx.

audit.reason: The arbitrary-set formulation is sound: restriction to S has total mass volume(S)=1 without requiring S measurable. Product integrability justifies Fubini; integration of constants gives u(x)−c = ∫(u(x)−u(y)), and the absolute-integral bound integrates to the stated inequality. The proof matches the standalone one-line type and needs no other child.

subproblem.title: The double-integral oscillation on Q_δ passes to L¹ limits of continuous functions
subproblem.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, Q₁ := {y ∈ Euclid n : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i}; fix δ ∈ ℝ with δ ≥ 0 and let Q_δ := {z ∈ Euclid n : δ < z_i < 1 − δ for all i} (Lebesgue measure). Let u : ℝⁿ → ℝ be integrable on Q₁, K ∈ ℝ, and let v_k : ℝⁿ → ℝ (k ∈ ℕ) be continuous functions with ∫_{x∈Q_δ}∫_{y∈Q_δ}|v_k(x) − v_k(y)| dy dx ≤ K for every k and ∫_{Q_δ}|v_k − u| → 0 as k → ∞. Then ∫_{x∈Q_δ}∫_{y∈Q_δ}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx ≤ K.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (u : Euclid (m + 1) → ℝ) (v : ℕ → Euclid (m + 1) → ℝ) (δ K : ℝ), IntegrableOn u {y : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1} → 0 ≤ δ → (∀ k, Continuous (v k)) → (∀ k, ∫ x in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, ∫ y in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, |v k x - v k y| ≤ K) → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, |v k x - u x|) atTop (𝓝 0) → ∫ x in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, ∫ y in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, |u x - u y| ≤ K
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 2 of the parent proof ("D(δ) ≤ D_k + 2ε_k, let k → ∞"), with the outputs of the sibling results smooth_approx/smooth_poincare replaced by the hypotheses on v_k, and with the integrability facts of step 1 of the parent proof written out.

Notation. n := m + 1, Euclid n with Lebesgue measure vol, S := Q_δ = {z : δ < z_i < 1 − δ for all i}, Q₁ = {y : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i}. All integrals are Bochner integrals; every integrand below is shown to be integrable, so they are genuine Lebesgue integrals.

1. S ⊆ Q₁. If z ∈ S then for each i, 0 ≤ δ < z_i and z_i < 1 − δ ≤ 1, using δ ≥ 0.
2. Boundedness. For y ∈ Q₁ each |y_i| < 1, so ‖y‖² = Σ_{i ∈ Fin n} y_i² ≤ Σ_{i ∈ Fin n} 1 = n (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq) and ‖y‖ ≤ √n. Hence S ⊆ Q₁ ⊆ B̄ := closedBall(0, √n). B̄ is compact (Euclid n is finite dimensional, hence proper), so vol(B̄) < ∞ and vol(S) ≤ vol(B̄) < ∞.
3. The measure μ. Let μ := vol restricted to S. By step 2, μ is a finite measure; put a := μ(univ) = vol(S), a real number ≥ 0. Since u is integrable on Q₁ ⊇ S, u ∈ L¹(μ). Each v_k is continuous, hence continuous on the compact set B̄ and therefore integrable on B̄ (ContinuousOn.integrableOn_compact); as S ⊆ B̄, v_k ∈ L¹(μ). Consequently, for every k, v_k − u ∈ L¹(μ), and ε_k := ∫ |v_k − u| dμ = ∫_{Q_δ}|v_k − u| is the quantity in the hypothesis, so ε_k → 0.
4. Fubini integrability. Fix k. On the finite product measure μ ⊗ μ, the functions (x, y) ↦ v_k(x) and (x, y) ↦ v_k(y) are integrable (Integrable.comp_fst / Integrable.comp_snd, using that μ is finite: by Tonelli ∫∫|v_k(x)| dμ(y) dμ(x) = a·∫|v_k| dμ < ∞, and both are a.e.-strongly measurable as compositions with coordinate projections). Hence G_k(x, y) := |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| is μ⊗μ-integrable, and by Fubini (Integrable.integral_prod_left) the function x ↦ ∫ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| dμ(y) is μ-integrable. Also x ↦ |u(x) − v_k(x)| is μ-integrable (step 3).
5. Pointwise triangle inequality. For all x, y: u(x) − u(y) = (v_k(x) − v_k(y)) + (u(x) − v_k(x)) + (v_k(y) − u(y)), hence |u(x) − u(y)| ≤ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| + |u(x) − v_k(x)| + |v_k(y) − u(y)|.
6. Inner integral. Fix x. The three functions of y on the right side of step 5 are μ-integrable: y ↦ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| (constant minus an integrable function, μ finite), the constant y ↦ |u(x) − v_k(x)| (μ finite), and y ↦ |v_k(y) − u(y)| (step 3). The left side y ↦ |u(x) − u(y)| is nonnegative. By monotonicity of the integral (integral_mono_of_nonneg: nonnegative left side, integrable right side, pointwise inequality) and linearity,
   ∫ |u(x) − u(y)| dμ(y) ≤ ∫ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| dμ(y) + a·|u(x) − v_k(x)| + ε_k,
   where the integral of the constant |u(x) − v_k(x)| equals μ(univ)·|u(x) − v_k(x)| = a·|u(x) − v_k(x)|.
7. Outer integral. The right side of step 6, as a function of x, is μ-integrable (step 4 plus a constant multiple of an integrable function plus a constant); the left side x ↦ ∫ |u(x) − u(y)| dμ(y) is nonnegative. Integrating step 6 over x with the same monotonicity and linearity, and using ∫ |u − v_k| dμ = ∫ |v_k − u| dμ = ε_k and ∫ ε_k dμ = a·ε_k:
   D(u) := ∫_{x∈S}∫_{y∈S}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx ≤ ∫_{x∈S}∫_{y∈S}|v_k(x) − v_k(y)| dy dx + a·ε_k + a·ε_k ≤ K + 2a·ε_k,
   the last step by the hypothesis on v_k.
8. Limit. Since ε_k → 0, K + 2a·ε_k → K + 2a·0 = K. As D(u) ≤ K + 2a·ε_k for every k, passing to the limit (ge_of_tendsto') gives D(u) ≤ K. ∎
proof_key_steps: δ ≥ 0 gives Q_δ ⊆ Q₁ ⊆ closedBall(0, √(m+1)); hence vol(Q_δ) < ∞, u is integrable on Q_δ, and each continuous v_k is integrable on Q_δ.
Fubini: (x, y) ↦ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| is integrable on Q_δ × Q_δ, so its inner integral is integrable in x.
Pointwise |u(x) − u(y)| ≤ |v_k(x) − v_k(y)| + |u(x) − v_k(x)| + |v_k(y) − u(y)|; integrating twice gives D(u) ≤ D(v_k) + 2 vol(Q_δ) ε_k ≤ K + 2 vol(Q_δ) ε_k.
Since ε_k = ∫_{Q_δ}|v_k − u| → 0, letting k → ∞ gives D(u) ≤ K.

audit.reason: All hypotheses match the exact type. Nonnegative δ gives containment in a compact enclosing ball, establishing finite measure and integrability of the continuous approximants. Fubini and two triangle-inequality integrations give D(u) ≤ K + 2 vol(Qδ) εk; convergence proves the conclusion. This also handles empty cubes without additional assumptions on K or δ. No undeclared dependency or circular step occurs.

subproblem.title: The open unit cube in Euclid (m + 1) has Lebesgue measure 1
subproblem.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ and n := m + 1. In ℝⁿ = Euclid n = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) with its Lebesgue measure (volume), the open unit cube Q₁ := {y : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i} has volume 1.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ m : ℕ, volume {y : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1} = 1
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: the notation paragraph of the parent proof ("vol(Q₁) = 1", obtained from the measure-preserving identification Euclid n ≃ (Fin n → ℝ)), written out in full.

Notation. m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, Euclid n = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) with volume = Lebesgue measure, y_i the i-th coordinate of y, Q₁ := {y ∈ Euclid n : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i}.

1. Let ofLp : Euclid n → (Fin n → ℝ) be the canonical map sending a Euclidean vector y to its coordinate function i ↦ y_i (so (ofLp y) i = y_i for all i). It is a measurable linear bijection, and by Mathlib's PiLp.volume_preserving_ofLp (a copy of EuclideanSpace.volume_preserving_symm_measurableEquiv_toLp) it is measure preserving from the volume of Euclid n to the volume of Fin n → ℝ, which is the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue measures.
2. Let B := {w : Fin n → ℝ : w i ∈ (0, 1) for all i} = ∏_{i ∈ Fin n} (0, 1) (Set.pi univ (fun _ => Ioo 0 1)). Since y_i = (ofLp y) i, a point y ∈ Euclid n lies in Q₁ if and only if ofLp y ∈ B. Hence Q₁ = ofLp⁻¹(B).
3. B is measurable, being a finite product of open intervals (MeasurableSet.univ_pi with measurableSet_Ioo). For a measure preserving map, the measure of the preimage of a measurable set equals the measure of the set (MeasurePreserving.measure_preimage). Therefore vol(Q₁) = vol(ofLp⁻¹(B)) = vol(B).
4. By the product formula for open boxes (Real.volume_pi_Ioo), vol(B) = ∏_{i ∈ Fin n} ofReal(1 − 0) = ∏_{i ∈ Fin n} 1 = 1.
5. Combining steps 3 and 4, vol(Q₁) = 1. ∎
proof_key_steps: The coordinate map ofLp : Euclid (m+1) → (Fin (m+1) → ℝ) is measure preserving (PiLp.volume_preserving_ofLp).
Q₁ = ofLp⁻¹(∏_i (0,1)), and the box is measurable, so vol(Q₁) = vol(∏_i (0,1)).

audit.reason: The one-line proposition exactly matches the prose. The coordinate map is measure preserving for the intended Euclidean volume; the measurable-box preimage calculation and product formula give volume 1. The proof is complete and independent.

subproblem.title: Exhausting the unit cube by the inner cubes Q_δ in the double-integral oscillation
subproblem.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, Q₁ := {y ∈ Euclid n : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i} and Q_δ := {z : δ < z_i < 1 − δ for all i} (Lebesgue measure). Let u : ℝⁿ → ℝ be integrable on Q₁ and K ∈ ℝ with ∫_{x∈Q_δ}∫_{y∈Q_δ}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx ≤ K for every δ ∈ (0, 1/2). Then ∫_{x∈Q₁}∫_{y∈Q₁}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx ≤ K.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (u : Euclid (m + 1) → ℝ) (K : ℝ), IntegrableOn u {y : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1} → (∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → δ < 1 / 2 → ∫ x in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, ∫ y in {z : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, δ < z i ∧ z i < 1 - δ}, |u x - u y| ≤ K) → ∫ x in {y : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1}, ∫ y in {y : Euclid (m + 1) | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1}, |u x - u y| ≤ K
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 3 of the parent proof (δ_j := 1/(j + 3) ↓ 0 and dominated convergence), carried out on the product space Q₁ × Q₁, where it becomes continuity of the integral along an increasing union.

Notation. n := m + 1, Euclid n with Lebesgue measure vol, Q(δ) := {z : δ < z_i < 1 − δ for all i}, Q₁ := {y : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i}. λ := vol ⊗ vol is the product measure on Euclid n × Euclid n. F(x, y) := |u(x) − u(y)| ≥ 0. Sibling used: unit_cube_volume (vol(Q₁) = 1).

1. Measurability. For every δ, Q(δ) = ⋂_{i ∈ Fin n} ({z : δ < z_i} ∩ {z : z_i < 1 − δ}). Each coordinate map z ↦ z_i is continuous, hence measurable, so each set in this finite intersection is measurable (measurableSet_lt) and Q(δ) is measurable. Products Q(δ) × Q(δ') are then λ-measurable.
2. Integrability on Q₁ × Q₁. By unit_cube_volume, vol(Q₁) = 1 < ∞, so ν := vol restricted to Q₁ is a finite measure, and u ∈ L¹(ν) by hypothesis. The restriction of λ to Q₁ × Q₁ is ν ⊗ ν (Measure.prod_restrict). On ν ⊗ ν the functions (x, y) ↦ u(x) and (x, y) ↦ u(y) are integrable (Integrable.comp_fst / Integrable.comp_snd, ν finite: by Tonelli ∫∫|u(x)| dν(y) dν(x) = ν(univ)·∫|u| dν < ∞, and both are a.e.-strongly measurable as compositions with coordinate projections). Hence F = |u(x) − u(y)| is integrable on Q₁ × Q₁ with respect to λ, and therefore also on every subset of Q₁ × Q₁.
3. The sequence of cubes. Let δ_j := 1/(j + 3) for j ∈ ℕ. Then 0 < δ_j ≤ 1/3 < 1/2, δ_j is nonincreasing in j, and δ_j → 0 (1/(j + 3) → 0). Put Q_j := Q(δ_j). If j ≤ k then δ_k ≤ δ_j, so z ∈ Q_j implies δ_k ≤ δ_j < z_i and z_i < 1 − δ_j ≤ 1 − δ_k for all i, i.e. Q_j ⊆ Q_k: the Q_j increase. Since δ_j > 0, also Q_j ⊆ Q₁.
4. ⋃_j Q_j = Q₁. The inclusion ⊆ is step 3. Conversely let x ∈ Q₁. For each i, x_i > 0 and 1 − x_i > 0; since δ_j → 0, eventually δ_j < x_i and eventually δ_j < 1 − x_i (i.e. x_i < 1 − δ_j). Because Fin n is finite, eventually these 2n conditions hold simultaneously (Filter.eventually_all), so x ∈ Q_j for some j.
5. Increasing product sets. Let s_j := Q_j × Q_j. By step 3, (s_j) is increasing, and each s_j is measurable (step 1). Since (Q_j) is increasing, ⋃_j (Q_j × Q_j) = (⋃_j Q_j) × (⋃_j Q_j) (a pair with x ∈ Q_a and y ∈ Q_b lies in Q_{max(a,b)} × Q_{max(a,b)}; Set.iUnion_prod_of_monotone), which equals Q₁ × Q₁ by step 4.
6. Fubini identification. For each j, F is λ-integrable on s_j ⊆ Q₁ × Q₁ (step 2), so Fubini's theorem for set integrals (setIntegral_prod) gives ∫_{s_j} F dλ = ∫_{x∈Q_j}∫_{y∈Q_j}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx =: D_j. Likewise, F being λ-integrable on Q₁ × Q₁, ∫_{Q₁×Q₁} F dλ = ∫_{x∈Q₁}∫_{y∈Q₁}|u(x) − u(y)| dy dx =: D.
7. Convergence. F is λ-integrable on ⋃_j s_j = Q₁ × Q₁ and the s_j are measurable and increasing, so ∫_{s_j} F dλ → ∫_{⋃_j s_j} F dλ (tendsto_setIntegral_of_monotone; equivalently dominated convergence, since 1_{s_j}F → 1_{Q₁×Q₁}F pointwise by step 5 with the integrable dominating function 1_{Q₁×Q₁}|F|). By steps 5 and 6 this says D_j → D.
8. Conclusion. Each δ_j lies in (0, 1/2) (step 3), so the hypothesis gives D_j ≤ K for every j. A limit of real numbers that are all ≤ K is ≤ K (le_of_tendsto'), hence D ≤ K, which is the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: Q_δ is measurable for every δ; by unit_cube_volume vol(Q₁) = 1, so |u(x) − u(y)| is integrable on Q₁ × Q₁ for the product measure.
With δ_j = 1/(j+3) ∈ (0, 1/2), the cubes Q_{δ_j} increase and their union is Q₁, so the products Q_{δ_j} × Q_{δ_j} increase to Q₁ × Q₁.
Fubini (setIntegral_prod) identifies D(δ_j) and D(Q₁) with set integrals over these product sets; continuity along increasing unions (tendsto_setIntegral_of_monotone) gives D(δ_j) → D(Q₁).
D(δ_j) ≤ K for all j, so the limit D(Q₁) ≤ K.

audit.reason: The exact type matches the prose. The sole declared dependency supplies finite unit-cube volume. Product integrability, measurable increasing cubes with δj = 1/(j+3), their product union, and Fubini satisfy the pinned set-integral convergence theorem. Passing the uniform bound to the limit proves precisely the conclusion.
